subtitle: Notice the unwritten habits that shape how your team works, tell a standard from a habit of perfectionism, and respond to mistakes in a way that keeps people willing to speak up.
audience: For all DHS and DSD staff who want practical ways to see and talk about the everyday norms on their team. It is not a performance review tool and does not replace HR guidance.

lessons.title: What culture means on a team
objectives: Describe workplace culture as the shared habits people follow when policy is silent.
Identify three places where a team's norms show: who speaks first, what gets praised and what gets quietly corrected.
Explain why a new colleague learns a team's norms by watching long before anyone explains them.
Recognize that the same habit can protect the people we serve in one place and slow the work in another.
lessons.teaching:
Culture is what people do when the policy is silent. Every team has written rules, and every team also has habits nobody wrote down: how fast you are expected to answer email, whether you can question a decision in a meeting, what happens when someone makes a small mistake. Edgar Schein, one of the best-known researchers on organizational culture, describes these habits as shared assumptions a group learns as it solves problems. Because they worked once, people stop noticing them.

You can see a team's culture in a few ordinary places. Who speaks first in a meeting, and who waits. What gets praised out loud, and what gets corrected in a side conversation. What a new person would be afraid to ask. None of these appear in a position description, yet they shape how the work gets done every day.

New colleagues learn culture by watching. They notice how a supervisor reacts to bad news and how coworkers talk about the people they serve. A single reaction, repeated a few times, can teach more than an orientation binder. That is why small moments matter so much.

Norms are not good or bad by themselves. Double-checking a benefits letter protects a family from a wrong amount or a missed deadline. Double-checking every routine email slows the team and teaches people to fear small errors. The useful question is not whether a habit is right, but whether it still serves the people the team supports.
lessons.keyPoint: Culture is what people do when the policy is silent. Notice the habit first, then ask whether it still serves the people your team supports.
lessons.example: Practice case: Three months into the job, the new colleague sends a client letter with one typo. Within an hour it comes up in a team chat, a reply-all and a one-on-one. Nobody is unkind. Since then, the new colleague asks three people to review every routine email before sending it. The case manager has noticed.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do?
choices: Say nothing, since extra checking cannot hurt.
Tell the new colleague that routine emails are fine to send without review.
Ask the new colleague what prompted the extra checks, then share which messages truly need a second look.
feedback: Extra checking has a cost. The new colleague's work slows, other people's time is used, and the habit of fear goes unnamed.
This is clear and kind. It may not reach the reason the new colleague started checking, so the fear can stay in place.
This names the norm, finds where it came from and gives the new colleague a clear line between a real standard and a fear of small mistakes.
lessons.reflection: Think about your first months on your current team. What did you learn by watching that nobody told you directly?
lessons.action: In your next team meeting, notice one moment that shows a team norm, such as who speaks first or how a question is received. Write it down in neutral words without naming anyone.

check.question: Which statement best describes workplace culture as this course uses the term?
check.correct: The shared habits and assumptions people follow when written policy does not say what to do.
wrong: The official mission statement and values posted by the agency.
The personal attitudes of the most senior person on a team.
check.feedback: Culture lives in everyday habits, especially where policy is silent. Mission statements matter, and leaders influence culture strongly, but culture is shared and learned by everyone on the team.

lessons.title: Standards, perfectionism and defensiveness
objectives: Distinguish a standard, which describes good work, from perfectionism, which treats any flaw as failure.
Describe how defensiveness can close a conversation before anyone learns what the concern is.
Explain how fear of mistakes can delay decisions for the people a team serves.
Use Tema Okun's description of perfectionism and defensiveness as a lens on habits, not as a label for a person.
lessons.teaching:
A standard says what good work looks like. A benefits notice must show the right amount, the right date and the right appeal rights. Standards protect people, and lowering them is not the goal of this course.

Perfectionism is different. It treats any flaw as a sign of failure, notices what is wrong far more than what is right, and links a person's worth to an error-free record. Tema Okun's widely used list of organizational habits names perfectionism and defensiveness among the patterns that can shape workplaces without anyone choosing them. Okun presents the list as a tool for reflection, not a way to accuse people. Read it here as a lens on habits, and keep the focus on what a team does rather than who someone is.

Defensiveness shows up when a concern is raised and the first move is to explain why it is not a problem. That reaction is human. When it becomes a team's habit, people stop raising concerns, and problems surface later and cost more.

The people we serve feel these habits even when they never see them. When staff fear mistakes, they slow down, hold decisions and avoid asking for help. A family waiting on an answer feels that delay. A test that helps: after a mistake, does the team learn, or does someone hide?
lessons.keyPoint: A standard describes good work. Perfectionism treats any flaw as failure. The test is what happens after a mistake: does the team learn, or does someone hide?
lessons.example: Practice case: The county partner tells the program manager that families say the team's letters are hard to understand. The letters follow the required template, and the program manager helped write it.
lessons.question: What is the program manager's best first response?
choices: Explain that the letters follow the required template.
Thank the county partner and ask which parts families find hard.
Promise to rewrite every letter right away.
feedback: This is true, and it closes the conversation before the program manager learns what families struggle with.
This keeps the concern open and gets the detail needed to act. Disagreement, if any, can come later, after understanding.
Well meant, but it commits before anyone understands the problem, and it may not be possible within the template rules.
lessons.reflection: When someone raises a concern about work you care about, what is your first reaction? What helps you stay curious instead of explaining?
lessons.action: The next time someone raises a concern with you, ask one question before you explain anything. Notice what you learn.

check.question: Which response is the clearest example of perfectionism rather than a standard?
check.correct: Treating a single typo in a routine email as evidence that a colleague is careless.
wrong: Checking a benefit amount against the case record before a notice goes out.
Agreeing as a team which documents need a second review.
check.feedback: Checking amounts and agreeing on review points are standards that protect people. Treating one small error as proof of a person's character is perfectionism, and it teaches people to hide mistakes.

lessons.title: Mistakes as information
objectives: Explain why most mistakes point to something in the process, not only to the person who made them.
Ask a question that looks for what made an error easy to make.
Describe the gap Amy Edmondson found between how many failures are truly blameworthy and how many are treated that way.
Recognize when an error does call for individual accountability.
lessons.teaching:
A mistake tells you something about the work. A wrong address on a notice may mean the template pulled from an old field, two systems disagree, or the step that should catch it was skipped during a rush. Asking what made the error easy to make leads to a fix that protects the next person. Asking who made it usually leads to more care for a week and then the same error again.

Amy Edmondson, who studies team learning, describes a spectrum of reasons things go wrong, from deliberate rule-breaking at one end to thoughtful experiments at the other. When she asks managers how many failures in their organizations are truly blameworthy, they usually say only a small share. When asked how many are treated as blameworthy, they say most. That gap teaches people to hide problems.

Edmondson's earlier research on hospital and work teams found that teams with a climate of psychological safety, a shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as admitting an error, reported more errors and learned more from them. Better teams were not making more mistakes; they were more willing to talk about them.

None of this removes accountability. Choosing to skip a required step, or a pattern that continues after support, still calls for a direct conversation and, when needed, the formal process. The point is to start with the process, so that individual accountability is used where it belongs.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask what made the error easy to make before you ask who made it. Most fixes live in the process.
lessons.example: Practice case: A client's appointment notice went out with the wrong office address. The client traveled to the old location and missed the appointment. The supervisor raises it at the next team meeting.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor ask first?
choices: "What in our process made this easy to miss?"
feedback: It finds the person, but not the step that made the error easy. The same error may happen again with someone else.
This treats the error as information and points the team toward a fix that protects the next client. The person who sent it can still be part of the conversation without being singled out.
It sounds reasonable, but it changes nothing in the process and adds pressure to everyone.
lessons.reflection: Think of the last mistake on your team. Was the conversation about the person or the process? What would a process question have found?
lessons.action: Choose one recurring error on your team. Write down the step where it usually happens and one change that would make it harder to make.

check.question: In Edmondson's research, what did teams with stronger psychological safety tend to do?
check.correct: Report and discuss more errors, which helped them learn and improve.
wrong: Make fewer errors because members were more afraid of consequences.
Avoid talking about errors so the team could stay positive.
check.feedback: Teams with more psychological safety were more willing to report errors, not more careless. Open discussion made learning possible.

lessons.title: Raising concerns and shifting a norm
objectives: Raise a concern by describing what you saw, why it matters and a question.
Receive a concern by thanking the person, asking one question and deciding what will change.
Rewrite a corrective message so it fixes the error and keeps learning open.
Name small, repeated actions that can shift a team norm over time.
lessons.teaching:
Raising a concern goes better with a simple pattern. Describe what you saw, say why it matters and ask a question. For example: "I noticed the letter went out with the old date. Families might miss the deadline. Can we look at how that step works?" This keeps the focus on the work and invites the other person into the fix.

Receiving a concern is a skill too. Thank the person, ask one question before you explain and decide what you will change. You can disagree later, after you understand. A supervisor who receives concerns this way teaches the whole team that speaking up is worth it.

Corrective messages matter. "This is the second time this week. Please be more careful." fixes nothing and adds fear. A better version names the issue, the impact and a next step: "The date on today's notice was last month's. Can you correct and resend it by noon? Let's look Thursday at why the template keeps pulling the old date."

Norms change through small acts repeated over time. Saying "I got that wrong" in a meeting. Thanking someone who catches your error. Asking a new colleague what surprised them about the team. What a supervisor praises, corrects or ignores teaches the most, but everyone on a team shapes its culture.
lessons.keyPoint: Describe what you saw, say why it matters and ask a question. Norms change through small, repeated acts.
lessons.example: Practice case: In last week's team update, the supervisor listed the wrong deadline for a report. The new colleague noticed but is not sure whether to say anything to someone more senior.
lessons.question: What is the best way for the new colleague to raise it?
choices: Stay quiet, since the supervisor will probably notice.
Message the supervisor: "I think the update says the 12th, but the form says the 15th. Should we send a correction?"
Reply-all to the team with the correct date.
feedback: Staying quiet protects the moment and risks people missing the real deadline.
This describes what was seen, why it matters and asks a question. It gives the supervisor an easy way to correct it, and it builds the habit of speaking up.
The correction is right, and doing it publicly before checking may embarrass the supervisor and confuse the team if the form is the one that is wrong.
lessons.reflection: What is one norm on your team you would keep, and one you would question? What small act could you try this month?
lessons.action: Pick one norm you noticed during this course. Write one sentence on whether it still serves the people your team supports, and one small act you will try.

check.question: Which message best fixes an error while keeping learning open?
check.correct: "The date on today's notice was last month's. Can you resend it by noon? Let's look Thursday at why the template keeps pulling the old date."
wrong: "This is the second time this week. Please be more careful."
check.feedback: A good corrective message names the issue, the impact and a next step, and looks at the process. Blame adds fear; brushing it off leaves the problem in place.

image.caption: The new colleague and the supervisor.

cards.back: The shared habits and assumptions people follow when written policy does not say what to do.
A clear description of what good work looks like, such as the right amount, date and appeal rights on a notice.
Treating any flaw as failure. It teaches people to hide mistakes instead of learning from them.
Explaining why a concern is not a problem before understanding it. Common and human, and costly as a team habit.
A shared belief on a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake or asking a question.
"What made this easy to miss?" It looks for the fix that protects the next person.

aid.heading: Notice your team's norms
items: What happens when someone makes a mistake?
Who gets credit, and for what?
What would a new person be afraid to ask?
Where did this habit start, and does that reason still apply?

aid.heading: Raise a concern
items: Say why it matters for the people we serve.
Ask a question that invites a fix.
Choose a private channel first when the concern is about one person.

aid.heading: Receive a concern
items: Ask one question before you explain.
Decide what you will change, and say when.

aid.heading: After a mistake
items: Ask what made it easy to make.
Fix the step, not just the instance.
Use individual accountability for deliberate or repeated choices, through the right process.

sources.title: Edgar H. Schein — Organizational Culture, American Psychologist (1990)
sources.note: Defines organizational culture as shared basic assumptions a group learns while solving problems. Supports the idea that habits persist after the problem they solved fades.

sources.title: Amy Edmondson — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
sources.note: The 1999 Administrative Science Quarterly article, hosted by MIT. Supports the definition of psychological safety and its link to team learning behavior.

sources.title: Amy C. Edmondson — Strategies for Learning from Failure, Harvard Business Review (2011)
sources.note: Describes a spectrum of reasons for failure and the gap between failures that are truly blameworthy and those treated as blameworthy.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: Source for perfectionism and defensiveness as organizational habits. Okun describes the list as a tool for reflection and cautions against using it to accuse people; it is not an empirical diagnostic instrument.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Respectful Workplace Policy 1432
sources.note: Statewide expectations for respectful conduct and routes for raising concerns. The course's conversation patterns support, and do not replace, these routes.
